name: Lengthened partials / stretch training
lead: Lengthened partials are repetitions performed only through the stretched portion of an exercise's range of motion, for example the bottom half of a curl or fly, rather than the full range. They are discussed in lifting communities as a way to emphasise the position in which the muscle is most elongated.

A general-purpose encyclopedic account of hypertrophy reports that full range of motion, especially at elongated muscle lengths, is described as enhancing growth more than partial range, and that partial-range training at longer muscle lengths is also said to promote hypertrophy, possibly through muscle damage [1].
The sources consulted for this entry do not summarise dedicated trials of lengthened partials.
infobox: Overload the stretched part of the range of motion

paras: Lifters using the technique either finish a set with extra partial reps in the lengthened range or build whole sets from them. Proponents link it to the idea that muscles grow well when loaded at long lengths.

Reviews of muscle hypertrophy describe mechanical tension as the currently accepted driver of growth and note that exercise at long muscle lengths is described as beneficial [1]. The sources used here do not summarise controlled trials comparing lengthened partials against full-range training.
No studies found specific to lengthened partials in the sources consulted. Broader hypertrophy literature touching on muscle length exists [1].

card.summary: Overloading only the stretched part of a rep; plausible in hypertrophy theory, thinly documented here.
card.note: Thin sources; no dedicated trials summarised.

quick.overview:
Lengthened partials are repetitions done only in the stretched portion of a lift. Lifters use them to load muscles at long lengths.

Hypertrophy overviews describe training at long muscle lengths as beneficial, but no dedicated trials were summarised here.
quick.mechanism: The technique aims to keep mechanical tension high while the muscle is elongated, which proponents link to growth.
quick.risks: Heavy loading in stretched positions can stress joints and connective tissue, as with other resistance training. No technique-specific harm data were identified.
